To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a novel saliency method, which we call Ablation Path S (APS) saliency, for black-box classification and that it is more accurate than state-of-the-art methods.

(1) we propose a novel approach to the saliency detection for image classification that is based on the idea of finding a path between two images that minimizes the difference between their predictions, (2) the path is found by solving a linear programming problem that can be solved in linear time, (3) we propose an efficient implementation of the algorithm that allows us to compute the saliency map for an image in less than a second on a modern CPU.

(i) the saliency map can be obtained using a simple gradient-based method and (ii) the saliencies of the input and the output layers of a convolutional neural network can be used to explain the decision of the network.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: What is the saliency of a given input for a given model? How can we quantify this saliency? How do salient regions differ for different models? What are the salient regions for a given model and a given input? How do saliency maps compare to human perception of saliency?
the question: what are the salient parts of the image that lead to a classification decision?
the following problem: Given a trained classification network, and a query image, what are the salient parts of the image for this classification task?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
salient regions are the regions that are most relevant to the decision made by the classifier.
the proposed method is a good method to detect saliency in images.
the saliency of an ablation path depends on the model, dataset, ablation, and metric, and that it can be used to understand the model, dataset or ablation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to identify the saliency of the ablation paths, which are a new type of saliency maps for black-box classifiers.
we can use adversarial examples as a proxy for saliency maps, which can be used for interpretability.

we propose an approach that is able to explain black-box classification models in terms of saliency maps and that we show that this is a valuable tool for understanding the models and the underlying data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
saliency is not a single concept, but rather a family of related notions.
salient parts of the input space for a given classifier are often located on the ablation path, i.e. the input space that leads from the current decision to a wrong one.
the saliency of the input can be learned from the model itself.
